title: Nash Equilibrium Existence via Nash's Brouwer Argument
description: Formalizes Nash's original 1950 proof that every finite multilinear game has a mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium. A single-valued continuous deviation map on the product simplex has a fixed point by Brouwer's theorem, and the fixed-point algebra shows no player can profitably deviate — avoiding the Kakutani/Berge set-valued machinery. 0 sorries; depends on one general Brouwer axiom in the parent file.

meta.historicalContext: John Nash's 1950 proof of equilibrium existence in his landmark 2-page paper used Brouwer's fixed point theorem directly — not Kakutani's generalization, which Nash also used in his 1951 Annals paper. The original argument defines a deviation map on the product simplex: each player shifts weight toward pure strategies that give higher expected utility, then normalizes. Continuous self-maps of compact convex sets have fixed points by Brouwer, and at any fixed point the deviation vanishes — meaning no player can unilaterally improve. This formalization implements this original argument for multilinear games.
meta.problemStatement: For a finite N-player game where expected utility is the multilinear extension of pure strategy payoffs (the standard definition for matrix games), does there exist a Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies? Nash (1950) proved yes, using Brouwer FPT applied to an explicit single-valued continuous self-map of the product simplex.
meta.proofStrategy: Define Nash's deviation map: for each player i and pure strategy k, compute the excess payoff from deviating to pure strategy k; shift weight toward strategies with positive excess, then normalize. This map is continuous (polynomial in strategy profiles) and maps the product simplex to itself. Brouwer FPT gives a fixed point, and the algebra of the fixed-point equation shows all excesses are zero — i.e., no player can improve by deviating.
meta.assumptions: 1 axiom: brouwer_pi_compact_convex (in BrouwerFixedPointOQ04.lean — general Brouwer FPT for products of compact convex sets in finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces). This file has 0 direct axioms; brouwer_product_simplex is now a theorem proved from the general axiom using mixed_strategy_nonempty, mixed_strategy_compact, and mixed_strategy_convex.

overview.historicalContext: Nash's original 1950 proof of equilibrium existence occupies only a paragraph in his 2-page PNAS paper. The key idea: define a continuous map on the product of mixed strategy simplices whose fixed points are Nash equilibria. Each player shifts weight toward pure strategies that offer improvement over their current mixed strategy. The normalization ensures the result is a valid mixed strategy. Brouwer's fixed point theorem guarantees a fixed point, and the algebra of the fixed-point equation implies all players are in equilibrium. Nash later gave a Kakutani-based proof in his 1951 Annals paper, but the Brouwer version is more direct and avoids upper hemicontinuity.
overview.problemStatement: For a finite N-player game with multilinear expected utility, prove that a Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies exists.
overview.proofStrategy: Define the excess payoff `excess_i(k, σ) = max(0, EU_i(eₖ, σ) − EU_i(σᵢ, σ))`, and the normalized Nash map `φᵢ(k, σ) = (σᵢ(k) + excess_i(k, σ)) / (1 + Σₗ excess_i(l, σ))`. Prove: (1) φ maps the product simplex to itself; (2) φ is continuous; (3) by Brouwer FPT, φ has a fixed point; (4) any fixed point is a Nash equilibrium.
keyInsights: Nash's map avoids UHC: the key innovation is replacing the set-valued best-response correspondence with a single-valued continuous map. No Berge's theorem needed.

Fixed point algebra: at a fixed point, each excess equals σᵢ(k) times the total excess Cᵢ. If Cᵢ > 0, all positive-weight pure strategies have positive excess, making the expected utility strictly larger than itself — contradiction.
Continuity from polynomials: the multilinear extension of payoffs is a polynomial in all strategy components, hence automatically continuous.
Product simplex is compact convex: the product of the mixed strategy simplices is compact (Tychonoff) and convex, satisfying Brouwer's hypotheses.

Historical conciseness: Nash's 1950 proof fits in one paragraph of a 2-page paper. The single-valued Brouwer map is far more elementary than the Kakutani/Berge route — it requires only polynomial continuity and compact convexity, not the machinery of set-valued analysis or upper hemicontinuity.
overview.text: Nash equilibrium existence for multilinear games via Nash's original Brouwer argument.

conclusion.summary: Formalizes Nash's original 1950 proof of equilibrium existence via Brouwer FPT. Main contributions: MultilinearGame structure, joint continuity of mixedUtility, Nash's deviation map, proof of mixedUtility_linear_in_i, algebraic proof that fixed points are Nash equilibria, and proof of brouwer_product_simplex from general brouwer_pi_compact_convex. 0 sorries, 0 local axioms (depends on general axiom in parent). Reduces OQ-01's 2 axioms to 1 general axiom.
conclusion.implications: Demonstrates that Nash equilibrium existence follows from the topological minimum (Brouwer FPT), without requiring the more subtle upper hemicontinuity theory of set-valued maps. The key obstacle (Berge's theorem) is replaced by elementary polynomial continuity.
openQuestions: Can brouwer_pi_compact_convex be proved from no_retraction_axiom + retraction_construction via a homeomorphism between compact convex bodies and closed balls?
Does the Nash map approach extend to games with infinite strategy sets (e.g., compact metric spaces)?

sections.title: Module Header and Imports
sections.summary: Module docstring framing the file as a formalization of Nash's 1950 Brouwer-based equilibrium proof, contrasted with the Kakutani route of OQ-01. Imports topology, inner-product spaces, convexity, and the parent BrouwerFixedPointOQ04 (source of the general Brouwer axiom). Opens namespace NashBrouwer.
sections.mathContext: Goal: $\forall$ finite multilinear game $G$, $\exists \sigma^* \in \prod_i \Delta_{m_i-1}$ that is a Nash equilibrium. Strategy: build a continuous self-map of the product simplex whose fixed points are equilibria.

sections.title: Part 1: Multilinear Game Structure
sections.summary: Defines the MultilinearGame structure (N players, per-player pure-strategy counts, pure payoffs) and mixedUtility — the multilinear extension of payoffs to mixed-strategy profiles.
sections.mathContext: $EU_i(\sigma) = \sum_{s \in \prod_j S_j} \Big(\prod_j \sigma_j(s_j)\Big)\, u_i(s)$ — a degree-$N$ polynomial in $\sum_i m_i$ variables.

sections.title: Part 2: Continuity of Mixed Utility
sections.summary: Proves mixedUtility is jointly continuous in the full strategy profile, as a finite sum of finite products of continuous coordinate projections — no compactness needed.
sections.mathContext: $EU_i$ is polynomial, hence continuous: a finite $\sum$ of finite $\prod$ of the continuous maps $\sigma \mapsto \sigma_j(s_j)$.

sections.title: Part 3: Linearity of Mixed Utility in Player i's Strategy
sections.summary: Proves mixedUtility_linear_in_i: holding the other players fixed, EU_i is linear (affine) in player i's own mixed strategy, by factoring player i's coordinate out of the multilinear sum via Finset.sum_comm and product splitting. (Now fully proved — no sorry.)

sections.title: Part 4: Nash's Deviation Map
sections.summary: Defines the excess payoff (gain from deviating to a pure strategy, clamped at 0) and the normalized Nash map that shifts weight toward improving strategies. Establishes well-definedness (denominator ≥ 1).

sections.title: Part 5: Nash Map Maps the Simplex to Itself
sections.summary: Proves nashMap sends the product simplex into itself: each component is non-negative and, for each player, the components sum to 1 — so the image is a valid mixed-strategy profile.

sections.title: Part 6: Nash Map is Continuous
sections.summary: Proves nashMap is continuous as a finite composition of continuous operations: the polynomial mixedUtility, max with 0, addition, and division by a denominator bounded below by 1 (never zero).
sections.mathContext: $\phi$ continuous: numerator and denominator are continuous and $1+\sum_l e_{il}\ge 1>0$, so the quotient is continuous everywhere on the simplex.

sections.title: Part 7: Fixed Points Are Nash Equilibria
sections.summary: The core argument: at a fixed point the equation rearranges to e_ik = σ_i(k)·C_i; if total excess C_i > 0 then every played strategy strictly improves, contradicting that EU_i is the average of those payoffs. Hence C_i = 0 and no deviation is profitable.
sections.mathContext: Fixed point $\Rightarrow e_{ik}=\sigma^*_i(k)\,C_i$. $C_i>0$ forces $EU_i(\sigma^*)>EU_i(\sigma^*)$, a contradiction; so $C_i=0$, i.e. $e_{ik}=0\ \forall k$ — equilibrium.

sections.title: Part 8: Brouwer FPT on the Product Simplex
sections.summary: Derives brouwer_product_simplex as a theorem from the general brouwer_pi_compact_convex axiom (in the parent file), using the proved facts that the product simplex is non-empty, compact, and convex.
sections.mathContext: $\prod_i \Delta_{m_i-1}$ is non-empty, compact (Tychonoff / closed-bounded in finite dim), and convex — exactly Brouwer's hypotheses — so any continuous self-map has a fixed point.

sections.title: Part 9: Nash Equilibrium Existence
sections.summary: Assembles the main theorem: nashMap is a continuous self-map of the compact convex product simplex, so it has a fixed point (Part 8), and every fixed point is a Nash equilibrium (Part 7) — therefore an equilibrium exists.
sections.mathContext: $\phi$ continuous self-map of compact convex $\prod_i\Delta_{m_i-1}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\exists\sigma^*=\phi(\sigma^*)$ $\Rightarrow$ $\sigma^*$ is a Nash equilibrium.

crossReferences.description: Provides the brouwer_pi_compact_convex axiom (general Brouwer FPT) from which brouwer_product_simplex is proved, and the kakutani_fixed_point_axiom used in OQ-01.

The Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem itself — every continuous self-map of a compact convex set has a fixed point. Nash's deviation map is exactly such a self-map of the product simplex, so equilibrium existence is a corollary of Brouwer.

Sperner's lemma is the combinatorial heart of Brouwer's theorem (proved via door counting). The Brouwer axiom this entry depends on is ultimately reducible to Sperner, giving the equilibrium proof a discrete combinatorial foundation.

Schauder's theorem extends Brouwer to compact convex subsets of infinite-dimensional spaces. It is the natural tool for open question 2 here — extending Nash's map argument to games with infinite (compact metric) strategy sets.

Von Neumann's minimax theorem for two-player zero-sum games is the special case of Nash equilibrium existence; both guarantee an equilibrium value, with the minimax theorem provable by LP duality rather than a fixed point.
